title: This Robot Speaks Ojibwe — and a Kid Built It!
summary: Have you ever pressed Tickle Me Elmo’s belly to hear him talk? Danielle Boyer had that toy as a kid, and it gave her a big idea. She wondered: Why aren’t there toys that speak Native American languages? So she invented the SkoBot — a tiny robot that sits on your shoulder and teaches you words in Anishinaabemowin. That’s a language spoken by the Ojibwe, Odawa, and Potawatomi people. But here’s the scary part: fewer than 10,000 people in the U.S. still speak it. In Canada, it’s about 25,000. Some Native languages have only a few dozen fluent speakers left. Boyer’s own grandmother is one of the last in their family to speak it. “You lose your culture, you lose a way to describe who you are,” she says. So Boyer, who is 25 and from the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians, started a nonprofit to help kids build their own SkoBots. One of those kids is 12-year-old Holden Hoy from Michigan. He programmed his robot, named Sabe (which means Bigfoot in Ojibwe), to answer questions. When you ask, “What’s your name?” it replies in his voice: “Hello. Sabe is my name. I was built by Holden Hoy. I will not take over the world. Or will I?” The robot isn’t really thinking — it just listens for a trigger word and plays a recording. But it’s a fun way to learn. At his school’s STEAM Museum, kids and parents crowded around his booth. “I’m happy they are learning things,” Holden said. “And I’m really happy that I’m part of the Ojibwe.”
why_it_matters: When a language disappears, we lose a part of human history—learning about them can help you appreciate your own family stories and traditions.

background_read: Many Native American languages are in danger because only a few elders speak them.
The Ojibwe people (a Native American group living around the Great Lakes) have passed down their language for thousands of years.
Today, devices like the SkoBot help young people learn these languages in a fun, hands-on way.
Article_Structure: WHO: Danielle Boyer, a 25-year-old inventor, and 12-year-old Holden Hoy
WHAT: They built a shoulder-sitting robot called the SkoBot that teaches Anishinaabemowin words using voice recordings
WHERE: At a school's STEAM Museum in Michigan
WHY: To help keep the Ojibwe language and culture alive because very few people still speak it fluently

perspectives.description: Kids and families feel excited to have a playful, interactive way to practice Ojibwe words every day.
Some worry that a robot cannot teach the deep cultural meanings and spirit behind the words.
See this as a clever tool to get young people interested in saving endangered languages.
